A revelation given in February 1831 outlined procedures for certain offenses, such as requiring two or more witnesses in cases of adultery. “Revelation, 23 February 1831 [D&C 42:74–93],”josephsmithpapers.org.
“Appendix 4: Declaration on Government and Law, circa August 1835 [D&C 134],” in Doctrine and Covenants, 1835 ed., 253,josephsmithpapers.org.

Most cases have been handled through a bishop’s court or high council. In early Church history, the Relief Society was also responsible to “watch over the morals—and be very careful of the character and reputation—of [its] members” (Emma Smith, in Relief Society Minute Book, Mar. 17, 1842, 13, Church History Library, Salt Lake City; Jill Mulvay Derr, Carol Cornwall Madsen, Kate Holbrook, and Matthew J. Grow, eds.,The First Fifty Years of Relief Society: Key Documents in Latter-day Saint Women’s History[Salt Lake City: Church Historian’s Press, 2016], 36). In keeping with that commission, Relief Society leaders exercised disciplinary authority and sometimes refused to admit individuals as members or dropped them for disciplinary reasons.
M. Russell Ballard, “A Chance to Start Over,”Ensign,Sept. 1990, 16.
